children.html: German translation and psychometric evaluation of the Body Appreciation Scale
Viren Swami a, *, Stefan Stieger b , Tanja Haubner c , Martin Voracek c

a Department of Psychology, University of Westminster, 309 Regent Street, London W1B 2UW, UK bCore Unit for Medical Education, Medical University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria c Department of Basic Psychological Research, School of Psychology, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria Received 20 June 2007; received in revised form 5 October 2007; accepted 13 October 2007

This paper examined the psychometric properties of the German version of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), a novel scale for the assessment of positive body image. Based on a community sample of 156 women and 144 men in Austria, results showed good internal reliability and construct validity for the BAS scores, as well as a unidimensional factor structure for both women and men. Specifically, Cronbach's alpha was high for both women (a = .90) and men (a = .85), and the BAS was correlated with the body esteem scale and self-esteem. In addition, women with lower BMIs reported greater body appreciation, but no such association was found for men. Finally, there were small sex differences in BAS scores, with men scoring more positively than women (Cohen's d = 0.26). The German BAS, a useful indicator of positive body image among Austrian adults, should prove valuable for the assessment of body image in German-speaking countries.

Keywords: Body Appreciation Scale; Positive body image; German translation; Validation; Community samples

Within the body image literature, the primary focus of research has been on the extent, and impact of, negative orientation towards one's own body (Cash, 2002). That is, although body image is acknowledged as a multi-dimensional construct (e.g., Thompson, Heinberg, Altabe, & Tantleff-Dunn, 1999), research has been limited by a pathology-oriented focus. Such an endeavour is important because the isolation of factors that promote positive body image may lead to more effective interventions for those with negative body image. To date, however, there remains a dearth of psychometric scales that explicitly measure positive

body image. To rectify this oversight, Avalos, Tylka, and Wood-Barcalow (2005) recently reported on the development and psychometric evaluation of a measure that explicitly examines positive body image, namely the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS). The BAS is a 13 item scale that measures four aspects of positive body image: (a) favourable opinions of one's own body; (b) acceptance of the body in spite of imperfections; (c)

supported undimensionality of the BAS, test-retest reliability of the BAS scores after 3 weeks, and several facets of construct validity, discriminant validity, incremental validity, and internal consistency reliability.

For the BAS to be useful in studies of positive body image, however, three extensions to the work of Avalos et al. (2005) are required. First, it would be beneficial to examine the psychometric properties of the BAS in internationally diverse populations, which the present study sought to achieve trough the development of a German translation of the BAS. Second, it is necessary to examine the validity of the BAS in relation to men's positive body image, which Avalos et al. did not report. Finally, given that Avalos et al. only examined college students, an additional purpose for the present study was to examine positive body image among a community sample. In short, the aim of the present study was to conduct a translation and validation of a German version of the BAS with male and female community samples.

Participants were a community sample of 156 women and 144 men, ranging in age from 16 to 80 years (age M \pm SD women = 31.66 \pm 13.60, men = 33.31 \pm = 15.05). Data collection took place in Vienna and its environs, and represents volunteers from the general population. The mean body mass index (BMI) for male

participants was 24.01 \text{ kg/m}^2 (SD = 3.34, range 17.81-36.92 \text{ kg/m}^2), whereas that of women was 21.94 \text{ kg/m}^2 (SD = 3.82, range 16.33-45.91 \text{ kg/m}^2), both of which fall within the normal BMI range (underweight: 15-18.5 \text{ kg/m}^2, normal: 18.5-24.9 \text{ kg/m}^2, overweight: 25.0-29.9 \text{ kg/m}^2). The majority of participants were Christians (81.0%; no religious affiliation = 16.3%). In terms of highest educational qualification, the majority of participants were educated to a secondary level (68.0%; university = 14.3%, apprenticeships = 10.3%, primary school = 7.0%).

the scale were created and presented to women and men, respectively. All items were rated on a 5-point scale (1 = never, 2= seldom, 3= sometimes, 4= often, 5 = always), with higher scores reflecting greater body appreciation. Responses on all 13 items were averaged to obtain an overall body appreciation score. The English version of the scale showed a unidimensional structure for women, remained reliable after a 3-week interval, and showed good construct, discriminant and incremental validities (Avalos et al., 2005).

This is a 35-item scale in which participants are asked to rate their feelings about various body parts and functions. Items are rated on a 5-point scale ranging from strong negative feelings to strong positive feelings. Means for each subscale were computed by taking the average of responses to items associated with each subscale. For both women and men, three subscales are computed, namely (1) physical attractiveness (PA) for men (in the present study, a = .89) or sexual attractiveness (SA) for women (a = .82); (2) upper body strength (UBS) for men (a = .86) or weight concern (WC) for women (a = .87), and (3) physical condition (PC) for both women (a = .80) and men (a = .89). Previous work has likewise shown that the scale has adequate internal consistency estimates and good construct validity (Franzoi & Shields, 1984).
Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSE; Rosenberg, 1965; German translation: von Collani & Herzberg, 2003)

The RSE is a brief, 10-item scale measuring selfworth, rated on a 4-point scale (1 = Strongly disagree, 4 = Strongly agree). Five items were reverse-coded prior to analysis, and an overall RSE score was computed by taking the average of responses to all items. The scale showed good internal consistency in the present study (women: a = .86, men: a = .82). Scores on both the English (Robinson & Shaver, 1973) and German RSE (Collani & Herzberg, 2003) demonstrate adequate internal consistency and convergent validity.

All participants were recruited opportunistically through a snowball-sampling technique. A number of data collectors, all of whom were study collaborators, directly recruited participants through their personal contacts. All participants completed the paper-andpencil questionnaire anonymously, and returned the

questionnaires in a sealed envelope. Participants were informed that the data would be prepared and analysed by an individual other than their contact in order to maintain the highest possible anonymity. Three researchers (TH, MV, SS) developed German versions of the BAS and BES scales from their originals in English, using the parallel blind technique (Behling & Law, 2000). In a first step, each researcher translated the questionnaire by herself or himself. The translations were then compared and disputable phrases or translations were settled.

So as to preserve internal validity, the data for women and men were analysed separately. Following Avalos et al. (2005), we conducted an exploratory factor analysis of the BAS data. The significance of Bartlett's test of sphericity [x2 (78) = 1204.72, p < .001] and the size of the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy (KMO = .92) revealed that the items of the BAS had adequate common variance for factor analysis (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2001). We, therefore, conducted a factor analysis with principal axis factoring and quartimax rotation (due to the expectance of a general factor; Pedhazur & Schmelkin, 1991) to examine the structure of BAS. The number of factors to be extracted was determined by factor eigenvalues above 1.0 and based on the scree-plot criterion. A one-factor solution produced an eigenvalue of 5.92 (45.5% of the variance explained). A two-factor solution yielded an eigenvalue of 1.12 (with an additional 8.6% of the variance explained), but no satisfactory solution was evident based on factor loadings. Item loadings on the singlefactor solution ranged from .40 to .88 (see Table 1), and thus provide support for the unidimensionality of the BAS (Tabachnick & Fidell).

Based on the results of the factor analysis, we calculated Cronbach's a for all 13 items of the BAS, and this revealed that the internal consistency of the BAS for female participants was very good (a = .90). Means, standard deviations, and Pearson r correlations of the measures for women (including BMI) are reported in Table 2. As can be seen, BAS showed a large positive correlation (cf. Cohen, 1992) with WC, moderate positive correlations with SA, PC, and self-esteem, and a moderate negative correlation with BMI. This provides support for the construct validity of the BAS.

For the male BAS data, the significance of Bartlett's test of sphericity [\chi^2(78) = 888.58, p < .001] and the size of the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy (KMO = .88) revealed that the BAS items had adequate common variance for factor analysis (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2001). The results of a factor analysis with principal axis factoring and quartimax rotation revealed a one-factor solution with an eigenvalue of 4.98 (38.3% of the variance explained). A two-factor solution was also possible (eigenvalue = 1.12, explaining an additional 8.6% of the variance), but as before, no satisfactory solution was evident based on factor loadings. Item loadings on the single-factor solution ranged from .38 to .88 (see Table 1), and thus provide support for the unidimensionality of the BAS (Tabachnick & Fidell).

Cronbach's \alpha for all 13 items of the BAS for men revealed that the internal consistency was good (\alpha = .85). Means, standard deviations, and Pearson r correlations of the measures for women (including BMI) are reported in Table 2. BAS showed large positive correlations (cf. Cohen, 1992) with PA, UBS and PC, and a moderate positive association with BMI, which provide support for the construct validity of the BAS. There was, however, no association between male body appreciation and BMI.
Before examining sex differences in BAS scores, we first sought to exclude any potential confounders.

One-way analyses of variance showed no significant sex differences in the mean age [F(1, 299) = 0.99, p > .05]and self-esteem [F(1, 299) = 0.15, p > .05]. There were, however, significant sex differences in mean BMI [F(1, 299) = 24.66, p < .05]. We, therefore, conducted a one-way analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) on BAS scores to investigate possible sex differences, with participants' BMI covaried out. The results of the ANCOVA showed a significant effect of sex [F(1,(299) = 9.09, p < .05; Cohen's d = 0.26], suggesting that men have a more positive body appreciation than women, irrespective of individual differences in BMI.

Hierarchical regressions were conducted with women and men separately to examine whether BAS predicts self-esteem above-and-beyond BES. In the first step of the regression, SA, WC, and PC (for women) or PA, UBS, and PC (for men) were entered as predictor variables, with RSE as the dependent variable. In the second step, BAS was entered in the regression equation to determine if it predicted selfesteem beyond the BES variables. For women, the final regression model was significant [F(4,155) = 5.88,p < .001, adjusted R^2 = .11, but only BAS (\beta = -.25, t = -2.58, p < .05, R^2 = 4\%) remained a significant predictor of self-esteem. Similarly for men, the final regression was significant [F(4,143) = 5.01, p < .05,adjusted R^2 = .10, with only BAS (\beta = -.27, t = -2.81, p < .05, R^2 = 4\%) significantly predicting self-esteem.

<sup>b</sup> The effect size reported is Cohen's d, and refers to the sex difference for mean scores on a given scale.

This is the first study to use a German translation of the BAS of Avalos et al. (2005). The results of the scale reliability tests showed that, for both women and men, this version of the scale had high inter-item reliability, which is consistent with the findings reported by Avalos et al. (2005). In addition, our results support the idea that the BAS scores show good construct validity, in this instance with body esteem and self-esteem. We were also able to provide evidence for a unidimensional factor structure of the BAS for both women and men in this sample. Finally, BAS was found to significantly explain incremental variance in self-esteem over-andabove that explained by negative body image (as measured by facets of the BES).

In general, therefore, the BAS appears to be a valid and reliable scale for the investigation of positive body image. The psychometric properties of both the English and German versions of the scale meet many of the desired statistical requirements for novel scales, which supports its use within psychological research. Moreover, as Avalos et al. (2005) have pointed out, the BAS benefits from ease of administration (taking only a few minutes to complete) and scoring. Furthermore, the present results suggest that the psychometric properties of the BAS hold when a community sample is investigated, as opposed to college women.

Our results also extend the work of Avalos et al. (2005) in several important ways. First, we have shown that the psychometric properties of the BAS, which Avalos et al. only reported for women, generalise to men. That is, the male BAS data demonstrated good internal reliability and construct validity, and also supported a unidimensional factor structure of the BAS (although the amount of variance explained by the single-factor structure was lower for men than it was for women). Before its use can be recommended for men, however, further tests will need to examine the psychometric properties of the BAS for men in different samples (e.g., among English-speaking groups) and using more diverse discriminant criteria (see below).

Second, we have shown that body appreciation is negatively correlated with women's BMI (a result predicted, but not tested by Avalos et al., 2005), but not significantly correlated with men's BMI. The former result is consistent with the idea that, in most socioeconomically developed settings, women's body image is intricately connected with the extent to which they conform to societal ideals of body weight (see Swami, 2007; Swami & Tove´e, 2005a). By contrast, the lack of a significant association between BAS and BMI

for men was puzzling, given that previous studies have reported linear or curvilinear associations between BMI and body satisfaction (e.g., Frederick, Peplau, & Lever, 2006; McCreary & Sadava, 2001). Our results may reflect the fact that in socioeconomically developed settings, men's physical attractiveness is more strongly related with upper-body muscularity than it is with BMI (Swami & Tove´e, 2005b), or may be due to sampling error.

Third, our preliminary findings appear to point to significant sex differences in BAS scores, even after controlling for individual differences in participants' BMI. That is, men appear to have more positive body appreciation than women. Although this finding would need to be replicated and substantiated, it nevertheless suggests that men may have greater access to societal and individual resources that promote positive body image. This may further reflect reports of greater body image dissatisfaction among women than men, at least until recently (see Calogero et al., in press). Finally, our results showed that the BAS accounted for incremental validity in self-esteem beyond that explained by factes of the BES, which is consistent with the suggestion of Avalos et al. (2005) that positive body image contains associations with well-being that are not completely overlapping with negative body image.

In addition to the limitations of the scale noted by Avalos et al. (2005, p. 295), our study is clearly limited in that the reliance on an opportunistic sample necessarily limits the generalisability of the present results. In addition, we did not counterbalance the order of presentation of the scales and only used a small number of additional scales to investigate the construct validity of the BAS. The choice of which scales to include was primarily governed by convenience, and although the general direction of our results is consistent with previous work, additional psychometric and statistical investigation of the BAS will be very useful (e.g., using parallel analysis; cf. Franklin, Gibson, Robertson, Pohlmann, & Fralish, 1995).

Future studies would also do well to examine the relationship between the BAS and other individual difference variables such as media exposure and dimensions of personality, which may yield interesting results. More generally, future work should seek to examine whether widely accepted theories within the body image literature (e.g., objectification theory, sociocultural theory) are useful predictors of positive body image. If the limitations discussed here and in Avalos et al. (2005) can be overcome, the BAS may prove a useful tool for stimulating research on positive body image.
